title: The Neurological Exam
summary: How to examine the nervous system systematically, from mental status to gait.

lessons.title: Mental Status

levels.kid:
When a brain doctor meets you, the first thing they check is how your thinking is working. This is called the mental status exam.

The doctor sees if you are awake and paying attention. They ask easy questions: What is your name? Where are we? What day is it? They might ask you to remember three words, like apple, table and penny, and say them again a few minutes later.

They listen to how you talk and if you can name things like a pen or a watch.

It is like checking that the main computer turns on before you test the keyboard and the mouse. If the thinking part is not working, the rest of the exam has to be read differently.
levels.hs:
The **mental status exam (MSE)** is the first part of the neurological exam, because everything else depends on it. A patient who is drowsy or confused cannot cooperate with strength or sensory testing.

Doctors move from basic to complex:
- **Level of consciousness**: alert, drowsy (lethargic), hard to wake (obtunded or stuporous), or unresponsive (coma).
- **Attention**: can the person focus? Tests include spelling WORLD backwards or saying the months of the year backwards.
- **Orientation**: do they know who they are, where they are, and the date?
- **Language**: is speech fluent? Can they understand commands, repeat a phrase, and name objects?
- **Memory**: registering three words, then recalling them after about five minutes.
- **Higher functions**: calculation, drawing a clock, copying shapes, judgment and abstraction (for example, explaining a proverb).

Order matters. If attention is poor, a person will fail memory tests even if their memory is normal, because the words never got in. That is why inattention points toward **delirium**, a sudden confusional state often caused by infection, medicines or metabolic problems, while slowly worsening memory with normal attention suggests **dementia**.

Screening tools like the MoCA or MMSE package these tests into a score.
levels.college:
The MSE is organized hierarchically: arousal enables attention, attention enables every higher domain. Testing out of order produces false localizations.

**Arousal** depends on the ascending reticular activating system (pontine and midbrain tegmentum, thalamic intralaminar nuclei) projecting to both hemispheres. Reduced arousal therefore means a brainstem/diencephalic lesion, bilateral hemispheric dysfunction, or a diffuse process (toxic-metabolic). A single unilateral cortical lesion does not cause coma unless it causes mass effect and herniation.

**Attention**: digit span (normal forward span is about 7, plus or minus 2), serial 7s, months backward, a continuous performance task (tap at each letter A). Inattention with acute onset and fluctuation is the core of **delirium**.

**Language**: test fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. These six items classify aphasias: Broca (nonfluent, comprehension relatively spared, poor repetition), Wernicke (fluent, paraphasic, poor comprehension and repetition), conduction (fluent, good comprehension, poor repetition), transcortical variants (repetition spared). Distinguish aphasia from **dysarthria**, which is a motor speech problem with normal language.

**Memory**: registration (immediate recall, really attention), delayed recall (episodic memory, hippocampal-medial temporal), cued recall and recognition. If cues rescue recall, the problem is retrieval (frontal-subcortical); if they do not, encoding/storage (hippocampal, as in Alzheimer disease) is suspected.

**Visuospatial and executive**: clock drawing, cube copy, Luria three-step sequence, verbal fluency (animals in 60 seconds), similarities. **Neglect** (line bisection, cancellation tasks) usually reflects right parietal lesions. Apraxia, agnosia and Gerstmann syndrome (dominant angular gyrus) are tested when cortical localization matters.
levels.phd:
The MSE is a structured probe of distributed networks, and its interpretation rests on the logic of dependency. Each domain is tested on top of intact lower domains, so a deficit is localizing only if the prerequisites are intact. This is the clinical analogue of a dissociation design: a patient who fails delayed recall but has a normal digit span and normal naming shows a relatively selective episodic memory deficit.

**Arousal versus content.** Plum and Posner separated the level of consciousness (arousal, brainstem-thalamic) from its content (cortical). The reticular activating system is not a single nucleus but cholinergic (pedunculopontine, laterodorsal tegmental), noradrenergic (locus coeruleus), serotonergic (raphe), dopaminergic and histaminergic (tuberomammillary) projections, plus orexin from the lateral hypothalamus, converging on thalamus and cortex. Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts can produce hypersomnolence with intact brainstem reflexes.

**Attention networks.** Posner's model distinguishes alerting, orienting (dorsal frontoparietal network, with the right hemisphere attending to both hemispaces) and executive control (anterior cingulate, lateral prefrontal). The right-hemisphere bias explains why neglect is more frequent and severe after right parietal or temporoparietal lesions.

**Memory taxonomy.** Episodic memory depends on the hippocampal-diencephalic circuit (hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus). Semantic memory degrades with anterior temporal atrophy (semantic dementia). Procedural memory relies on basal ganglia and cerebellum and survives amnesia, as famously shown in patient H.M.

**Psychometrics.** Screening instruments trade depth for speed. The MMSE has ceiling effects in highly educated people and floor effects in low-literacy groups, and poorly samples executive function; the MoCA is more sensitive to mild cognitive impairment but less specific. Scores are influenced by education, language and culture, so a cutoff is a probability shift, not a diagnosis.
levels.expert:
On the wards the MSE starts the moment you walk in: is the patient awake, tracking you, talking, picking at the sheets? Most of the exam is done before you formally test anything.

**Practical sequence for a consult**: arousal (and what stimulus it takes), attention (months backward is quick and robust), orientation, language (spontaneous speech, a two-step command, repetition of a sentence, naming of low-frequency items like a watch buckle), recall of three or five words, and a quick visuospatial task. Document exactly what the patient did, not just a score: "named 2 of 5 objects, paraphasic errors" is more useful to the next clinician than "MoCA 21".

**Pitfalls an attending watches for**
- Calling an aphasic patient "confused". Fluent aphasia with jargon can look like delirium; check comprehension with a nonverbal command and look for a field cut or other focal sign. A new aphasia is a stroke until proven otherwise and may be a code stroke.
- Labeling inattention as dementia. Delirium is common in hospitalized older adults, often hypoactive (quiet, sleepy) and frequently missed. Tools like the CAM (acute onset and fluctuation, inattention, plus disorganized thinking or altered consciousness) help.
- Ignoring the nondominant hemisphere. Neglect and anosognosia (unawareness of deficit) after right hemisphere strokes can make a patient appear well while they ignore half of space.
- Testing in the wrong language, without glasses or hearing aids, or right after sedation.

**Neurosurgical relevance**: serial MSEs track patients after head injury, subarachnoid hemorrhage or tumor resection; a subtle drop in attention or a new drowsiness can be the first sign of hydrocephalus, rebleeding, vasospasm or rising pressure. Awake craniotomy for tumors near language cortex uses real-time naming tasks during cortical stimulation to map and protect eloquent areas. Always compare against the patient's own baseline.

keyPoints: The mental status exam comes first: arousal → attention → orientation, language, memory, higher functions.
Poor attention invalidates memory testing; acute inattention with fluctuation suggests delirium.
Coma needs brainstem/thalamic, bilateral hemispheric or diffuse dysfunction, not a small unilateral cortical lesion.
Language testing: fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading, writing; aphasia is not dysarthria.
Cues rescuing recall suggests a retrieval problem; failed cueing suggests hippocampal encoding failure.
Neglect usually points to the right (nondominant) parietal lobe.

examples.src: Patient fluent but cannot repeat "no ifs, ands or buts"; comprehension good.
examples.tr: Conduction aphasia pattern (classically arcuate fasciculus / supramarginal region).

examples.src: Elderly inpatient, sleepy, cannot say months backward, worse at night, started two days ago.
examples.tr: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattentive. Search for infection, drugs, metabolic causes.

examples.src: Recalls 0/3 words, even with category cues and multiple choice.
examples.tr: Encoding/storage failure, typical of medial temporal (hippocampal) disease.

test.q: Which part of the mental status exam must be assessed first?
test.explain: Arousal comes first: a drowsy patient cannot be validly tested on any higher domain.

test.q: A patient cannot say the months of the year backward. Which domain is mainly impaired?
test.explain: Months backward is a classic attention task.

test.q: Why can poor attention cause a false 'memory' deficit?
choices: The words were never registered, so they cannot be recalled
test.explain: If information is not registered, failure to recall it does not prove a memory disorder.

test.q: Acute onset, fluctuating course and inattention best describe:
test.explain: These are the core features of delirium; dementia is usually gradual with attention preserved early.

test.q: A patient speaks fluently with made-up words and cannot follow commands. Most likely:
test.explain: Wernicke aphasia: fluent, paraphasic speech with poor comprehension (and poor repetition).

test.q: Slurred speech with perfectly normal word choice, grammar and comprehension is:
test.explain: Dysarthria is a motor speech problem; language itself is intact.

test.q: A patient ignores the left side of the page in a cancellation task. The lesion is most likely in the:
test.explain: Hemispatial neglect most often follows right parietal (temporoparietal) lesions.

test.q: Which isolated lesion is LEAST likely to cause coma by itself?
test.explain: A small unilateral cortical lesion does not impair arousal unless it causes mass effect.

test.q: Delayed recall improves with category cues. This suggests:
test.explain: If cues help, the memory was stored but hard to retrieve, a frontal-subcortical pattern.

test.q: Which quick drawing task tests planning and visuospatial skill (two words)?
test.explain: Clock drawing tests visuospatial and executive function.

test.q: Fluent speech, good comprehension but poor repetition = ___ aphasia.
test.explain: Conduction aphasia spares fluency and comprehension but impairs repetition.

test.q: Name the hemispheric side usually damaged in neglect (left or right).
test.explain: Right hemisphere attends to both sides of space, so right lesions cause more severe neglect.

test.q: Sudden confusion from infection or medicines in a hospitalized older adult is called ___.
test.explain: Delirium is an acute confusional state, often reversible.

kidTest.q: What does the mental status exam check?
kidTest.explain: It checks how your thinking and brain are working.

kidTest.q: What does the doctor check first?
choices: If you can draw a clock
kidTest.explain: Being awake comes first; everything else needs it.

kidTest.q: The doctor asks you to remember three words. What is being tested?
kidTest.explain: Remembering words later tests memory.

kidTest.q: Saying the months backward tests…
kidTest.explain: It needs focus, so it tests attention.

kidTest.q: Fill in: Where are we? What day is it? These check if you know where and ___ you are. (hint: time word)
kidTest.explain: Orientation means knowing who, where and when you are.

kidTest.q: Why check thinking before the rest of the exam?
choices: It is like turning on the computer before testing the mouse
kidTest.explain: If thinking is off, the other tests cannot be trusted.

advancedTest.q: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts most typically produce:
choices: Hypersomnolence/reduced arousal with vertical gaze problems
advancedTest.explain: Paramedian thalamic territory (often from one artery of Percheron) affects intralaminar arousal systems and vertical gaze.

advancedTest.q: Why is neglect more severe after right than left hemisphere lesions?
choices: The right hemisphere attends to both hemispaces, the left mainly to the right
The left hemisphere has no parietal lobe
It is not; they are equal
advancedTest.explain: Right-hemisphere dominance for spatial attention means the left hemisphere cannot compensate for left space.

advancedTest.q: Procedural learning surviving severe amnesia (as in H.M.) shows that:
choices: Procedural memory relies on systems such as basal ganglia and cerebellum
advancedTest.explain: Memory systems dissociate: declarative is hippocampal-dependent; procedural is not.

advancedTest.q: A post-op tumor patient becomes slightly drowsier and less attentive over hours. The best interpretation:
choices: Possible early sign of rising pressure, hydrocephalus or bleeding: urgent reassessment and imaging
advancedTest.explain: Subtle arousal or attention decline is an early warning in neurosurgical patients and warrants prompt evaluation.

lessons.title: Cranial Nerve Exam

levels.kid:
Cranial nerves are twelve special wires that come straight out of your brain, not your spinal cord. They work your eyes, face, ears, mouth and neck.

A doctor checks them with fun little tests. Follow my finger with your eyes. Smile big. Puff out your cheeks. Squeeze your eyes shut. Stick out your tongue. Shrug your shoulders. The doctor might shine a light in your eyes to watch your pupils get small.

If one of these moves does not work, the doctor gets a clue about which wire, or which part of the brain stem, has a problem. It is like checking each light switch in a house to find the broken one.
levels.hs:
There are **12 cranial nerves (CN I–XII)**. Most leave the brainstem, and each has a quick bedside test:
- **CN I (olfactory)**: smell, tested with a familiar scent (often skipped).
- **CN II (optic)**: visual acuity, visual fields (comparing with the examiner's fields), pupil response, and looking at the back of the eye with an ophthalmoscope.
- **CN III, IV, VI**: eye movements. III moves the eye up, down and in, lifts the eyelid and constricts the pupil; IV (trochlear) helps look down and in; VI (abducens) moves the eye outward.
- **CN V (trigeminal)**: facial sensation and chewing muscles; the corneal reflex.
- **CN VII (facial)**: facial expression: raise eyebrows, close eyes tight, smile.
- **CN VIII (vestibulocochlear)**: hearing and balance.
- **CN IX and X**: palate rises evenly when saying "ah", gag reflex, swallowing, voice.
- **CN XI (accessory)**: shoulder shrug and head turning.
- **CN XII (hypoglossal)**: tongue movement; a weak tongue points toward the weak side.

The **pupillary light reflex** uses CN II as the input and CN III as the output. A "blown" (large, unreactive) pupil in a patient after head injury can mean CN III is being compressed by a shifting brain, a neurosurgical emergency.
levels.college:
**Visual pathway (CN II)**: test acuity per eye, fields by confrontation, and fundi (papilledema, optic atrophy). Field patterns localize: monocular loss (eye/optic nerve), bitemporal hemianopia (chiasm, e.g. pituitary tumor), homonymous hemianopia (retrochiasmal). A **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)**, found with the swinging flashlight test, indicates an optic nerve lesion: both pupils dilate when light swings to the affected eye.

**Ocular motor (III, IV, VI)**: check primary position, pursuit in an H pattern, saccades, and ask about diplopia. CN III palsy: eye "down and out", ptosis, and in compressive lesions (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) a dilated pupil, because pupillomotor fibers run superficially. Ischemic (diabetic) III palsies often spare the pupil. CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia worse looking down and in; head tilts away from the affected side. CN VI palsy: failure to abduct; a false localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure.

**CN V**: three divisions (V1, V2, V3) for sensation; jaw deviates toward the weak pterygoid. Corneal reflex: afferent V1, efferent VII.

**CN VII**: an upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to upper face); a lower motor neuron lesion (Bell palsy) weakens the whole half-face, sometimes with hyperacusis and taste loss.

**CN VIII**: whisper test, Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests separate conductive from sensorineural loss.

**IX/X**: uvula deviates away from the weak side. **XI**: sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side; trapezius shrugs. **XII**: tongue deviates toward the weak side; atrophy and fasciculations suggest a lower motor neuron lesion.
levels.phd:
The cranial nerve exam is a precise localizer because nuclei and fascicles occupy fixed brainstem levels: III and IV in the midbrain, V through VIII in the pons (V spanning the whole brainstem), IX through XII in the medulla. Combining a cranial nerve deficit with long-tract signs fixes a lesion in three dimensions.

**Pupillary physiology.** The light reflex runs retina, optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, then (bypassing the lateral geniculate) to pretectal nuclei, which project bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei; parasympathetic fibers travel with CN III to the ciliary ganglion. Bilateral pretectal projection explains the consensual response and why a pure afferent defect never causes anisocoria. Anisocoria greater in light implicates the parasympathetic limb; greater in darkness implicates sympathetic failure (Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, with or without anhidrosis, a three-neuron chain from hypothalamus through the cervical cord, lung apex and carotid sheath).

**Ocular motor control.** Horizontal gaze is generated in the pontine paramedian reticular formation and abducens nucleus, which contains both motor neurons and internuclear neurons crossing via the **medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)** to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus. An MLF lesion produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia: impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye, convergence often preserved. Add the abducens nucleus and you get the one-and-a-half syndrome. Vertical gaze is organized in the rostral midbrain (riMLF, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, posterior commissure); dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome produces upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation and convergence-retraction nystagmus.

**Facial nerve anatomy.** The corticobulbar supply to the upper facial nucleus is substantially bilateral, though primate tracing suggests the story involves multiple cortical motor areas rather than a simple bilateral rule. The nerve's long course through the internal acoustic meatus, facial canal and parotid gland generates distinctive combinations (stapedius, chorda tympani, greater petrosal) that localize along its path.
levels.expert:
A bedside cranial nerve exam takes about three minutes if it is systematic, and it is the part of the exam most likely to tell you the lesion is in the brainstem.

**How seniors actually do it**: look at the face first (ptosis, pupil asymmetry, facial droop, head tilt). Then fields by confrontation, pupils with the swinging light, pursuit in an H with a question about double vision, saccades, facial sensation in all three divisions, facial strength including the forehead, finger rub hearing, palate and voice, shrug and head turn, tongue. Fundoscopy every time headache or visual symptoms are present.

**Red flags in neurosurgery**
- A new painful CN III palsy with a dilated pupil: posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise; urgent CT angiography.
- A unilateral fixed dilated pupil with falling consciousness after trauma: uncal herniation; this is a time-critical surgical decision, not a reason to wait for more tests.
- Bilateral CN VI palsies with headache and papilledema: raised intracranial pressure (tumor, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension).
- Bitemporal field loss: pituitary or sellar mass; check endocrine function and consider pituitary apoplexy if sudden.
- Lower cranial nerve weakness (IX, X, XII) with dysphagia: aspiration risk; protect the airway and get a swallow assessment before feeding.

**Common traps**: calling a Bell palsy a stroke or vice versa (check the forehead, but remember a pontine lesion of the facial nucleus or fascicle also weakens the forehead), mistaking a pharmacologically dilated pupil (eye drops) for a CN III palsy (it will not constrict with weak pilocarpine), and missing a subtle RAPD.

**Operative relevance**: skull base and posterior fossa surgeons monitor facial and lower cranial nerves intraoperatively with electromyography, and a careful pre-op cranial nerve exam is the baseline you will be judged against.

keyPoints: 12 cranial nerves; III–IV midbrain, V–VIII pons, IX–XII medulla.
Pupillary light reflex: afferent CN II, efferent CN III (parasympathetic).
CN III palsy: down and out, ptosis; a dilated pupil suggests compression (aneurysm, herniation).
Upper motor neuron facial weakness spares the forehead; Bell palsy does not.
RAPD (swinging flashlight) indicates an optic nerve lesion.
Tongue deviates toward the weak side; uvula deviates away from the weak side.

examples.src: Right eye down and out, right ptosis, dilated right pupil, severe headache.
examples.tr: Compressive right CN III palsy, e.g. posterior communicating artery aneurysm: emergency.

examples.src: Left eye cannot adduct on right gaze; right eye has nystagmus; convergence normal.
Right face weak including forehead, taste change on right tongue.
examples.tr: Right lower motor neuron facial palsy (e.g. Bell palsy), proximal to the chorda tympani branch.

test.q: Which cranial nerve is the efferent (output) limb of the pupillary light reflex?
test.explain: CN II senses light; parasympathetic fibers in CN III constrict the pupil.

test.q: An eye that is 'down and out' with ptosis indicates a palsy of:
test.explain: CN III supplies most eye muscles and the eyelid lifter; unopposed IV and VI pull the eye down and out.

test.q: Which cranial nerve abducts (moves outward) the eye?
test.explain: Abducens (VI) innervates the lateral rectus.

test.q: Forehead-sparing facial weakness suggests:
choices: Upper motor neuron (e.g. cortical stroke) lesion
test.explain: The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, so UMN lesions spare the forehead.

test.q: Bitemporal hemianopia localizes to the:
test.explain: Crossing nasal fibers at the chiasm carry temporal field information; pituitary tumors compress them.

test.q: In the swinging flashlight test, both pupils dilate when light moves to the left eye. This means:
choices: Left relative afferent pupillary defect (optic nerve problem)
test.explain: Reduced afferent input from the left optic nerve causes paradoxical dilation: an RAPD.

test.q: The tongue deviates to the right on protrusion. Which hypoglossal nerve is weak?
test.explain: The intact genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side.

test.q: The uvula deviates to the left. Which vagus nerve is weak?
test.explain: The uvula is pulled away from the weak side, toward the strong side.

test.q: A unilateral blown pupil after head injury with falling consciousness suggests:
test.explain: The herniating uncus compresses CN III and its superficial pupillary fibers.

test.q: Which cranial nerve number is the trochlear nerve? (Roman or Arabic)
test.explain: Trochlear is CN IV, supplying the superior oblique.

test.q: The corneal reflex afferent is CN V and the efferent is CN ___.
test.explain: Touching the cornea (V1) triggers blinking via the facial nerve (VII).

test.q: Name the syndrome of ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
test.explain: Horner syndrome reflects loss of sympathetic supply to the eye and face.

test.q: Bilateral CN ___ palsies are a 'false localizing' sign of raised intracranial pressure.
test.explain: The long intracranial course of the abducens makes it vulnerable to raised pressure.

kidTest.q: How many cranial nerves are there?
kidTest.explain: There are twelve cranial nerves.

kidTest.q: Cranial nerves come out of the…
kidTest.explain: They leave the brain and brainstem directly.

kidTest.q: 'Follow my finger' tests the nerves that move your…
kidTest.explain: Eye-movement nerves are tested by following a target.

kidTest.q: Shining a light in your eyes makes the pupils…
kidTest.explain: Light makes the pupils get smaller.

kidTest.q: Smiling and puffing your cheeks tests the nerves for your ___.
kidTest.explain: The facial nerve moves the face.

kidTest.q: Checking each nerve is like…
choices: Checking each light switch to find the broken one
kidTest.explain: Each test checks one wire.

advancedTest.q: Impaired left eye adduction on right gaze, right abducting nystagmus, normal convergence. Lesion?
advancedTest.explain: Left INO: the left MLF lesion blocks the signal to the left medial rectus; convergence uses a separate pathway.

advancedTest.q: Anisocoria greater in darkness points to:
advancedTest.explain: In darkness the normal pupil dilates but the sympathetically denervated one cannot, widening the asymmetry.

advancedTest.q: Why can a diabetic (ischemic) CN III palsy spare the pupil?
choices: CN III has no pupillary fibers
Pupillary fibers lie superficially and keep collateral blood supply; ischemia hits the core
The pupil is controlled by CN II
advancedTest.explain: Microvascular ischemia affects the central nerve; superficial pupillomotor fibers are spared, unlike with compression.

advancedTest.q: Upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation and convergence-retraction nystagmus suggest:
choices: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome, e.g. pineal tumor or hydrocephalus
advancedTest.explain: Dorsal midbrain compression disrupts vertical gaze centers and the pretectal light-reflex pathway.

lessons.title: Motor & Reflex Exam

levels.kid:
Your muscles get their orders from the brain through two kinds of messengers. The first messenger runs from the brain down the spinal cord. The second runs from the spinal cord out to the muscle.

A doctor checks your muscles by looking at them, feeling how loose or stiff they are, and asking you to push and pull against their hand.

Then comes the fun part: the reflex hammer! A gentle tap below your knee makes your leg kick all by itself. That kick is a shortcut loop through your spinal cord.

If the kick is too big or too small, the doctor learns which messenger might be broken.
levels.hs:
The motor exam has five parts: **inspection, tone, power, reflexes and coordination** (coordination is covered in the next lesson).

- **Inspection**: muscle wasting (atrophy), twitching under the skin (**fasciculations**), and abnormal movements like tremor.
- **Tone**: the resistance felt when the examiner moves a relaxed limb. Increased tone can be **spasticity** or **rigidity**; decreased tone is **flaccidity**.
- **Power**: graded 0 to 5 on the MRC scale. 0 = no movement, 1 = flicker, 2 = moves with gravity removed, 3 = moves against gravity, 4 = against some resistance, 5 = normal.
- **Reflexes**: tapping a tendon stretches the muscle and triggers a loop through the spinal cord. Key reflexes: biceps (C5–C6), brachioradialis (C6), triceps (C7), knee (L3–L4), ankle (S1).

The key idea is **upper vs lower motor neuron**. Upper motor neurons run from the cortex to the spinal cord; damage (stroke, spinal cord injury) causes weakness with **increased tone, brisk reflexes and an upgoing big toe (Babinski sign)**. Lower motor neurons run from the spinal cord to the muscle; damage (nerve injury) causes weakness with **wasting, fasciculations, low tone and reduced reflexes**.
levels.college:
**Upper motor neuron (UMN) syndrome**: weakness in a pyramidal pattern (arm extensors and leg flexors weaker than their antagonists), spasticity that is velocity-dependent and shows a "clasp-knife" catch, hyperreflexia, spread of reflexes, clonus (rhythmic beats after a sustained stretch), Hoffmann sign in the hand, and an extensor plantar response (**Babinski sign**). In acute UMN lesions (spinal shock, acute stroke) tone and reflexes may initially be low.

**Lower motor neuron (LMN) syndrome**: weakness in the distribution of the root, nerve or anterior horn cells, atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia and hyporeflexia or areflexia; plantar responses flexor or absent.

**Extrapyramidal rigidity** differs from spasticity: it is velocity-independent, present in flexors and extensors equally ("lead-pipe"), with superimposed tremor giving "cogwheeling" in parkinsonism. **Paratonia** (gegenhalten) is involuntary resistance that increases with the examiner's effort, seen in frontal lobe disease and dementia.

**Pronator drift**: arms extended, palms up, eyes closed; a subtle UMN lesion causes the weak arm to pronate and drift down. It is one of the most sensitive bedside signs of a mild corticospinal lesion.

**Reflex grading** (0 absent, 1+ reduced, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk with spread, 4+ with sustained clonus). Reinforcement (Jendrassik maneuver: clenching teeth or pulling hooked fingers) brings out reflexes that seem absent. Asymmetry is more meaningful than absolute values.

**Root levels to memorize**: biceps C5/6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, finger flexors C8, patellar L3/4 (mainly L4), Achilles S1. **Superficial reflexes**: abdominal (T8–T12, lost in UMN lesions), cremasteric (L1–L2), anal wink (S2–S4).
levels.phd:
The monosynaptic stretch reflex is the simplest circuit in the nervous system and its gain is a readout of descending control. Muscle spindle Ia afferents synapse directly on homonymous alpha motor neurons; the same afferents inhibit antagonist motor neurons through Ia inhibitory interneurons (reciprocal inhibition). Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity.

**Why UMN lesions cause hyperreflexia.** The corticospinal tract is only part of the picture. Pure pyramidal tract lesions in primates (medullary pyramidotomy) produce weakness and loss of fine finger control, and a Babinski sign, but little spasticity. Spasticity arises from loss of parapyramidal (corticoreticulospinal) inhibitory control with relative preservation of facilitatory vestibulospinal and medial reticulospinal input. Over weeks, spinal circuits reorganize: reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia terminals, decreased reciprocal and recurrent (Renshaw) inhibition, motor neuron persistent inward currents (serotonergic and noradrenergic modulation of L-type Ca2+ and Na+ currents), and collagen changes in muscle. This time course explains the initial flaccidity of spinal shock.

**The Babinski sign** is a release phenomenon. The normal adult plantar response is flexor; in infants, before corticospinal myelination, the response is extensor. Toe extension is part of a flexion withdrawal synergy (extensor hallucis longus is physiologically a flexor of the limb, shortening it), which the corticospinal tract normally suppresses.

**Fasciculations** arise from spontaneous discharges of a motor unit, often generated in distal motor axons. Benign fasciculations are common in healthy people; in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis they come with weakness, atrophy and electrophysiological denervation. ALS is the classic disease that mixes UMN and LMN signs in the same region, the combination that the revised El Escorial and Gold Coast criteria formalize.
levels.expert:
On a busy service the motor exam answers three questions in a few minutes: is there weakness, what pattern is it, and is it UMN or LMN?

**Efficient routine**: look at both sides exposed (wasting, fasciculations, asymmetry), pronator drift, tone at arms and legs (a quick roll of the leg and lift at the knee catches spasticity), confrontational strength comparing left with right in key muscles (deltoid, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger abduction, hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion), then reflexes and plantar responses. Grade weakness honestly; 4/5 covers a huge range, so many clinicians use 4-, 4, 4+ or describe function ("can't rise from a chair without arms").

**Pattern recognition**
- Pyramidal-pattern weakness with brisk reflexes in one arm and leg: a brain lesion on the opposite side, or a high cervical cord lesion on the same side.
- Brisk reflexes in the legs but not arms, with a sensory level: thoracic cord.
- Brisk legs, brisk arms, but a reduced biceps reflex with an inverted brachioradialis: compressive myelopathy at C5–C6 (the reflex arc is broken at that level, but signs below are UMN).
- Wasting, fasciculations, and brisk reflexes in the same limb: think motor neuron disease.
- Proximal symmetric weakness with normal reflexes and sensation: myopathy.

**Neurosurgical context**: a patient with cervical stenosis and new hand clumsiness, Hoffmann signs and gait change has myelopathy that may need decompression; the exam determines urgency. After spinal trauma the ASIA (ISNCSCI) exam, with motor scores in ten key muscles per side and sacral sparing, defines completeness and prognosis and must be done carefully and repeated.

**Traps**: pain-limited or effort-dependent ("give-way") weakness, a stiff limb from arthritis mistaken for spasticity, and a missing ankle jerk in older adults that may be normal for age.

keyPoints: UMN lesions: weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski sign.
LMN lesions: weakness, wasting, fasciculations, low tone, reduced or absent reflexes.
MRC power scale: 0 none, 3 against gravity, 5 normal.
Reflex roots: biceps C5–6, triceps C7, knee L3–4, ankle S1.
Rigidity is velocity-independent (lead-pipe, cogwheel); spasticity is velocity-dependent (clasp-knife).
Pronator drift is a sensitive sign of a mild UMN lesion; early spinal shock can look like LMN.

examples.src: Left arm and leg weak, brisk left reflexes, left Babinski.
examples.tr: Right hemisphere or right brainstem corticospinal lesion (above the decussation).

examples.src: Hand wasting and fasciculations plus brisk knee reflexes and Babinski signs.
examples.tr: Mixed UMN and LMN signs: consider motor neuron disease (ALS) or cervical myelopathy with root involvement.

examples.src: Absent ankle reflex and weak foot plantarflexion with back pain radiating down the leg.
examples.tr: S1 radiculopathy (LMN pattern at a single root).

Pyramid lesions cause flaccid paralysis forever

lessons.title: Sensory & Coordination Exam

levels.kid:
Your skin has tiny helpers that feel touch, pain, hot, cold and buzzing. Your body also has a secret sense that tells you where your arms and legs are, even with your eyes shut. Try it: close your eyes and touch your nose!

A doctor tests feeling with a soft cotton touch, a cold tuning fork, and a buzzing tuning fork on your toe.

Then they test coordination, which is how smoothly your body moves. They ask you to touch your nose, then their finger, back and forth. The part of the brain called the cerebellum is like the coach that keeps every move smooth and on target.
levels.hs:
**Sensation** travels in two main pathways, and the exam tests both:
- **Spinothalamic tract**: pain and temperature. Tested with a pin (a clean, disposable one) and a cold object. These fibers cross to the other side of the spinal cord almost immediately.
- **Dorsal columns**: vibration, fine touch and **proprioception** (knowing joint position). Tested with a 128 Hz tuning fork on the big toe and by moving the toe up or down while the patient's eyes are closed. These fibers stay on the same side until the brainstem.

Testing usually starts at the toes and moves up, because many nerve problems (like diabetic neuropathy) affect the longest nerves first in a **"stocking-glove"** pattern. A **sensory level** across the trunk, where feeling changes below a line, points to the spinal cord.

**Coordination** depends mostly on the **cerebellum**:
- **Finger-to-nose**: overshooting (dysmetria) or a tremor that gets worse near the target (intention tremor).
- **Heel-to-shin**: sliding the heel down the opposite shin.
- **Rapid alternating movements**: flipping the hand quickly; clumsiness is called dysdiadochokinesia.

A key rule: cerebellar problems show up on the **same side** as the lesion.

The **Romberg test** (standing feet together, then closing eyes) checks proprioception: falling only when the eyes close means the person was relying on vision to make up for lost position sense.
levels.college:
**Primary modalities**: light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, joint position. Map deficits against dermatomes, peripheral nerve territories and patterns:
- **Length-dependent polyneuropathy**: distal symmetric, stocking then glove (the glove appears when leg involvement reaches about the knee).
- **Mononeuropathy**: one nerve's territory (e.g. median: thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger).
- **Radiculopathy**: a dermatome, often with pain.
- **Myelopathy**: a sensory level; dissociated loss in partial cord syndromes (Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss and weakness, contralateral pain/temperature loss a couple of segments below).
- **Brainstem/thalamus/cortex**: hemisensory loss; crossed face-body loss in the lateral medulla.

**Cortical sensation** (requires intact primary modalities): two-point discrimination, **stereognosis** (identifying an object by touch), **graphesthesia** (numbers drawn on the palm), and **extinction to double simultaneous stimulation**. Deficits suggest contralateral parietal cortex.

**Cerebellar signs**: midline (vermis) lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia with relatively normal limb testing; hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, rebound, hypotonia, and nystagmus. Cerebellar dysarthria is "scanning" or ataxic.

**Romberg**: a positive Romberg (stable with eyes open, falls with eyes closed) indicates **sensory ataxia** from proprioceptive loss (dorsal columns, large-fiber neuropathy, dorsal roots). In cerebellar ataxia the patient is unsteady even with eyes open, so Romberg is not "positive" in the strict sense. Always guard the patient.

**Limits**: sensory testing is the most subjective part of the exam; repeat inconsistent findings and correlate with objective signs (reflexes, wasting, nerve conduction).
levels.phd:
Somatosensation is organized into parallel channels whose anatomy creates the clinical patterns. Large myelinated Aβ afferents from Meissner, Pacinian, Merkel and Ruffini endings and muscle spindles enter medially, ascend ipsilaterally in the gracile and cuneate fasciculi, synapse in the dorsal column nuclei, cross as internal arcuate fibers and ascend in the medial lemniscus. Small Aδ and C fibers enter laterally (Lissauer tract), synapse in laminae I, II and V of the dorsal horn, and second-order axons cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments to form the anterolateral system. Both reach the ventral posterior thalamus (VPL for the body, VPM for the face) and then S1, while spinothalamic projections also reach insula and cingulate for affective pain.

**Somatotopy creates patterns.** In the dorsal columns, sacral fibers lie medial and cervical lateral; in the spinothalamic tract, sacral fibers lie lateral. Intrinsic cord lesions can therefore spare sacral pinprick sensation (sacral sparing), an important sign of intramedullary disease and, in trauma, of an incomplete injury. A central cord lesion (syrinx) interrupts crossing fibers in the anterior commissure, producing a cape-like, suspended dissociated loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch.

**Coordination as prediction.** The cerebellum is modeled as a forward-model and error-correction system: mossy fibers convey context and efference copy, climbing fibers from the inferior olive signal errors, and Purkinje cells adjust output through deep nuclei. Dysmetria and intention tremor reflect failed prediction of limb dynamics, with oscillatory corrections near the target. Cerebellar hemispheres project via the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle to contralateral thalamus and motor cortex, whose output then recrosses in the corticospinal tract, the double crossing that makes cerebellar signs ipsilateral.

**Sensory ataxia versus cerebellar ataxia** differs in visual compensation: proprioceptive loss can be offset by vision, so the deficit grows with eye closure, the logic of Romberg's original observation in tabes dorsalis.
levels.expert:
Sensory examination is where junior clinicians lose the most time and gain the least information. Senior clinicians do a focused sensory exam guided by the question.

**Focused routine**: screen vibration and joint position at the great toes, pinprick ascending from the foot until it becomes normal (and compare proximal with distal in the arms), check for a sensory level on the trunk front and back when a cord lesion is possible, and test perianal sensation when cauda equina or conus problems are on the table. Draw the findings; a diagram beats a paragraph.

**High-yield patterns**
- Back pain, bilateral leg symptoms, urinary retention and saddle numbness: cauda equina syndrome until imaging says otherwise; emergency MRI and neurosurgical review.
- A sensory level at the nipple line (T4) or umbilicus (T10) with leg weakness: thoracic cord compression; metastatic disease is a common culprit in older adults.
- Lost vibration and proprioception with a positive Romberg and brisk reflexes but absent ankle jerks: think B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) or copper deficiency.
- Hemisensory loss splitting exactly at the midline, with inconsistent findings: consider a functional disorder, but only after objective signs are excluded and with positive features documented.

**Coordination pearls**: test limb coordination in weak patients cautiously, because weakness causes clumsiness that is not ataxia. Watch the heel-shin test for wobble rather than speed. A patient who cannot stand with feet together even with eyes open has truncal ataxia, which, if sudden, may be a cerebellar stroke or hemorrhage. A swelling cerebellar lesion can compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem, causing hydrocephalus and requiring urgent neurosurgical decompression; that is why sudden vertigo with inability to walk is never assumed to be benign.

keyPoints: Dorsal columns: vibration, proprioception, fine touch; cross in the medulla.
Spinothalamic: pain and temperature; cross within 1–2 segments in the cord.
Stocking-glove = length-dependent neuropathy; sensory level = spinal cord.
Positive Romberg (falls only with eyes closed) = sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia.
Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause IPSILATERAL limb ataxia; vermis lesions cause gait/truncal ataxia.
Cortical sensation (stereognosis, graphesthesia, extinction) tests the parietal lobe.

examples.src: Right leg weak with lost vibration on the right, lost pinprick on the left below T10.
Loss of pain and temperature across both shoulders and arms, touch preserved.
examples.tr: Central cord lesion such as a syrinx (cape distribution, dissociated loss).

examples.src: Overshoots target with left finger-to-nose, clumsy left rapid alternating movements.
examples.tr: Left cerebellar hemisphere lesion (ipsilateral limb ataxia).

test.explain: The anterolateral spinothalamic system carries pain and temperature.

test.explain: Midline cerebellar lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia.

test.explain: Dysdiadochokinesia is a cerebellar sign.

test.explain: A sensory level localizes to the spinal cord.

test.explain: Graphesthesia tests parietal cortical sensation.

test.q: Saddle numbness with urinary retention suggests ___ equina syndrome.
test.explain: Cauda equina syndrome is a neurosurgical emergency.

kidTest.q: Close your eyes and touch your nose. This uses your sense of…
kidTest.explain: That hidden sense is called proprioception.

kidTest.q: The buzzing tool the doctor puts on your toe is a…
kidTest.explain: A tuning fork tests buzzing (vibration) feeling.

kidTest.q: Which brain part is the coach for smooth moves?
kidTest.explain: The cerebellum keeps movements smooth and on target.

kidTest.q: Touching your nose, then the doctor's finger, tests…
kidTest.explain: It checks smooth, accurate movement.

kidTest.q: A cold tuning fork checks if you can feel hot and ___.
kidTest.explain: Temperature feeling includes hot and cold.

kidTest.q: Your skin has helpers that feel…
kidTest.explain: Skin sensors feel touch, pain, temperature and vibration.

advancedTest.q: Why are cerebellar hemisphere signs ipsilateral?
choices: The cerebellum controls spinal cord directly without crossing
Cerebellar output crosses to the opposite thalamus/cortex, and the corticospinal tract crosses back
advancedTest.explain: Double crossing (superior cerebellar peduncle decussation, then pyramidal decussation) makes signs ipsilateral.

advancedTest.q: Preserved perianal pinprick in a patient with otherwise severe cord injury indicates:
choices: Sacral sparing, suggesting an incomplete injury with better prognosis
advancedTest.explain: Sacral sparing means some long-tract fibers survive.

advancedTest.q: A cape-like loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch is most consistent with:
choices: Syringomyelia interrupting crossing fibers in the anterior commissure
advancedTest.explain: A central cord cavity cuts crossing spinothalamic fibers at those levels.

advancedTest.q: Lost vibration/proprioception, positive Romberg, brisk knees, extensor plantars and absent ankle jerks. Best first lab target?
advancedTest.explain: This is the pattern of subacute combined degeneration; B12 (and copper) deficiency should be checked.

lessons.title: Gait

levels.kid:
Walking looks easy, but it needs your whole nervous system working as a team: the brain plans, the cerebellum balances, the spinal cord passes messages, the nerves carry them, and the muscles do the work.

That is why a doctor loves to watch you walk. They might ask you to walk normally, walk on your tiptoes, walk on your heels, and walk heel-to-toe like on a tightrope.

Different problems make different walks. Some people shuffle with tiny steps. Some wobble like they are on a boat. Some swing one stiff leg around in a half circle. Each walk is a clue that tells the doctor where to look.
levels.hs:
Watching someone walk is one of the most informative parts of the neurological exam, because walking needs strength, sensation, balance, coordination and automatic control from the basal ganglia.

The doctor watches the patient stand up from a chair, walk, turn, and then walk on toes, on heels, and in tandem (heel-to-toe).

Classic gaits:
- **Hemiparetic (spastic) gait**: after a stroke, one stiff leg swings out in a half circle (**circumduction**) and the arm is held bent.
- **Parkinsonian gait**: stooped posture, short shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, trouble starting, and turning in many small steps; sometimes the steps speed up (festination) or freeze.
- **Cerebellar (ataxic) gait**: wide-based, unsteady, staggering, like being drunk; tandem walking is impossible.
- **Sensory ataxic gait**: high-stepping and slapping the feet down, much worse in the dark or with eyes closed.
- **Steppage gait**: foot drop makes the person lift the knee high so the toes clear the ground (often a peroneal nerve or L5 root problem).
- **Waddling gait**: the hips drop side to side because hip muscles are weak, as in many muscle diseases.

Walking on heels tests ankle dorsiflexion (L4–L5); walking on toes tests plantarflexion (S1).
levels.college:
Gait analysis integrates every level of the neuraxis, and many gait disorders are recognizable at a glance.

**Systematic observation**: base width, stride length, cadence, arm swing, posture, initiation and turning, foot clearance, trunk sway, and the effect of eye closure (Romberg) and of cognitive dual-tasking (talking while walking).

**Patterns and localization**
- **Spastic hemiparetic**: circumduction, reduced knee flexion and foot drop on the affected side; contralateral corticospinal lesion.
- **Spastic paraparetic (scissoring)**: stiff legs crossing over, toe-walking; bilateral corticospinal disease such as cervical myelopathy, hereditary spastic paraplegia or cerebral palsy.
- **Parkinsonian**: hypokinetic, narrow-based shuffle with freezing and en bloc turns; basal ganglia.
- **Frontal ("magnetic") gait / higher-level gait disorder**: broad-based, feet seem stuck to the floor, start hesitation, often with cognitive decline and urinary urgency. Classic in **normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)** and small vessel disease. Arm swing is often preserved, unlike Parkinson disease ("lower-body parkinsonism").
- **Cerebellar**: wide-based, irregular steps and trunk titubation; unsteady with eyes open or closed.
- **Sensory ataxic**: stamping, watching the feet, markedly worse with eyes closed; dorsal columns or large-fiber neuropathy.
- **Steppage**: foot drop from common peroneal neuropathy, L5 radiculopathy or distal neuropathy.
- **Waddling (Trendelenburg)**: proximal hip girdle weakness; myopathy or bilateral superior gluteal nerve problems.
- **Antalgic**: shortened stance on a painful limb.

**Functional gait disorders** show inconsistency, improvement with distraction, and patterns incompatible with anatomy; they are diagnosed on positive signs, not merely by exclusion.

Simple timed tests (Timed Up and Go, 10-meter walk) quantify gait and help track change after treatment.
levels.phd:
Locomotion is generated hierarchically. Spinal **central pattern generators** produce rhythmic alternating flexor-extensor activity even without supraspinal input, as shown in decerebrate and spinalized animal preparations. The **mesencephalic locomotor region**, including the pedunculopontine and cuneiform nuclei, initiates and scales locomotion through reticulospinal pathways. The basal ganglia gate this system: output from the GPi and SNr tonically inhibits the brainstem locomotor centers, and dopamine depletion increases that inhibition, contributing to hypokinesia and freezing. The cerebellum, especially the vermis and fastigial nuclei, regulates posture, interlimb coordination and step timing through vestibulospinal and reticulospinal outputs, while the cortex (supplementary motor area, premotor and parietal areas) adapts gait to goals and obstacles.

**Freezing of gait** in Parkinson disease likely reflects failed integration of motor, cognitive and limbic inputs at the basal ganglia-brainstem interface. It worsens at doorways and turns and under cognitive load, and can be overcome by external cues (visual lines, rhythmic auditory cues), which may route control through cerebellar-premotor circuits instead of the basal ganglia. Freezing often responds poorly to dopaminergic treatment, and PPN stimulation has been tried with mixed results.

**Normal pressure hydrocephalus** illustrates the frontal-subcortical gait syndrome. The proposed mechanisms include stretching and ischemia of periventricular white matter fibers (including those from the supplementary motor area and leg representations near the ventricles), impaired CSF dynamics and glymphatic clearance. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, a narrow callosal angle and crowding of high convexity sulci (DESH). The physiology remains debated, which is reflected in imperfect predictors of shunt response.

**Quantitative gait analysis** (pressure walkways, inertial sensors, motion capture) measures stride-to-stride variability, which predicts falls and cognitive decline better than average speed, and has made gait a candidate "vital sign" for neurological aging.
levels.expert:
Watch the patient walk from the waiting room if you can; it is the most honest part of the exam.

**Bedside protocol**: rise from a chair with arms crossed, walk at least 10 meters, turn, walk back, then tandem, heels, toes, Romberg, and a pull test for postural reflexes (stand behind the patient and be ready to catch them). Ask about falls, near-falls and fear of falling.

**Clinical pearls**
- A new inability to walk is an emergency in disguise. Sudden truncal ataxia may be a cerebellar stroke; new leg weakness with back pain or bladder change needs urgent spinal imaging.
- In the NPH triad (gait disturbance, cognitive decline, urinary urgency or incontinence), gait comes first and is the feature most likely to improve. Neurosurgeons often use a large-volume lumbar tap test or an extended lumbar drain, measuring gait before and after, to predict response to a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. The gait measurement is the outcome.
- Lower-body parkinsonism with preserved arm swing and a broad base suggests vascular disease or NPH rather than Parkinson disease, and it usually responds poorly to levodopa.
- Bilateral foot drop with a steppage gait suggests a polyneuropathy or a lumbar canal process; unilateral foot drop needs a careful exam to distinguish peroneal nerve, L5 root and sciatic nerve (inversion weakness implicates L5 or sciatic, since the tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve).
- Cervical myelopathy often first presents as a subtly stiff, unsteady gait with hand clumsiness; it is easy to blame on age.

**Postoperative and rehab practice**: gait speed and Timed Up and Go are used to document outcomes after spine surgery, shunting and deep brain stimulation. Always ask physical therapy for their assessment; their gait observations are often more detailed than ours.

keyPoints: Walking tests the whole neuraxis: cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum, cord, nerves, muscles.
Hemiparetic gait: circumduction; parkinsonian: shuffling, reduced arm swing, freezing.
Cerebellar gait: wide-based and unsteady even with eyes open; sensory ataxia worsens with eyes closed.
Steppage gait = foot drop (peroneal nerve, L5, neuropathy); waddling = proximal hip weakness.
NPH triad: gait (magnetic), cognition, urinary; tap test predicts shunt response.
Heel walking tests dorsiflexion (L4–L5); toe walking tests plantarflexion (S1).

examples.src: Elderly patient, broad-based gait with feet seemingly stuck to the floor, urinary urgency, slowed thinking; large ventricles on CT.
examples.tr: Suspect normal pressure hydrocephalus; consider a tap test for shunt candidacy.

examples.src: Shuffling, stooped, freezes at doorways, reduced right arm swing, rest tremor.
Right foot slaps, knee lifted high, weak dorsiflexion and eversion but normal inversion.
examples.tr: Common peroneal (fibular) neuropathy, e.g. at the fibular head.
